name: Eyebrowmaxxing

lead:
Eyebrowmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for optimising the brows. Forum users treat the eyebrows as a frame for the eyes: their thickness, how low they sit, and the angle of the tail are said to change how alert, masculine or approachable a face reads.
The usual route is grooming, which means removing stray hairs such as a unibrow or hairs below the tail. Some people add growth routines such as castor oil, while others turn to cosmetic tattooing or brow transplants. Evidence comes mostly from community guides and before-and-after threads; Wikipedia describes the grooming and procedure options in general terms.

paras: In community threads, people shape brows with tweezers, a razor, threading or waxing, usually taking away hairs at the middle and under the tail while leaving the upper line. Some follow a guide that uses landmarks drawn from the nose to the eye corner to decide where the brow should end. Others apply oils to encourage growth, fill sparse brows with cosmetics, or have follicles transplanted or pigment tattooed in. Results from grooming are visible straight away; growth routines are described over weeks to months.

Plucking or waxing too much can leave sparse patches, and users worry about ingrown hairs and brows that look noticeably done. Transplants and cosmetic tattooing carry the usual procedure risks (infection, uneven results) and are performed by professionals. Posters on forums also disagree about which shapes look best, so outcomes vary with the individual face.

angle.text: Grooming changes brow shape immediately, and cosmetics, tattooing or transplants can add density where it is sparse. Practitioners say a lower, fuller and cleaner brow frames the eyes and strengthens the upper face.

lead: Eyebrowmaxxing, also written browmaxxing, is a looksmaxxing term for deliberately shaping and improving the eyebrows. Practitioners treat the brows as a frame for the eyes: how thick they are, how low they sit and how the tail angles are said to affect how alert, intense, masculine or friendly a face appears.[1][2] Because brow changes are quick and inexpensive compared with most facial work, the topic is a standard part of grooming-focused "softmaxxing" discussion.[3]

The methods run from ordinary grooming to procedures. Everyday grooming includes tweezing, threading, waxing and shaving, which reshape the brow line and remove a unibrow.[4] Sparse brows can be filled in with pencils, powders and gels, tattooed with microblading-style cosmetic tattooing, or rebuilt with follicle transplants taken from the back of the head.[4][5][6] On looksmax.org, threads discuss castor oil for growth, share step-by-step shaping guides and post transformation photos that combine brow work with other changes.[7][8][9]

Biologically, eyebrows keep sweat and debris out of the eyes, and a 2018 study summarised by Wikipedia argued that their main role is communication, since mobile brows signal emotions such as recognition and sympathy.[4] That communicative role is why practitioners focus on brow position: published rating studies show that raising or lowering the brow changes how faces are judged on attractiveness, masculinity, dominance and trustworthiness.[10][11] Brow fashion has also swung between eras, from the painted high brows of Japanese hikimayu to the thin plucked brows of the 1920s and 1930s.[4][12] No published clinical study has examined eyebrowmaxxing as a practice, but there is research on brow perception, transplantation, cosmetic tattooing and the grooming options it draws on.

paras: The eyebrow is a band of short terminal hairs above each eye, following the lower margin of the brow ridge. Wikipedia describes tweezing as the most common grooming method, with waxing growing in popularity and threading, trimming and shaving also used, and notes that brows can be darkened with permanent dye or shaved and redrawn.[4] Eyebrowmaxxing groups these ordinary options under one aim: arranging density, shape and position so the brow supports the rest of the face.[1]

Community guides emphasise brow position relative to the eye. A poster in one thread advised taking hairs only from the upper edge so the brow stays as low set as possible,[2] while another thread describes a landmark method, drawing a line from the nose to the corner of the eye and trimming hairs that fall under it, to keep a neutral-to-positive tilt.[13] A longer guide that other posters recommend as a reference covers shape, tools and common mistakes.[7]

The topic sits inside the wider looksmaxxing culture that Wikipedia describes as an online self-improvement practice that grew from forum communities in the 2010s and spread to TikTok in the 2020s. In that account grooming belongs to the non-invasive "softmaxxing" end of the spectrum, and "hunter eyes", a feature standard that includes low-set eyebrows, a positive canthal tilt and little upper eyelid exposure, is one of the facial ideals discussed.[3]

Users describe tweezing, trimming with a razor, threading and waxing. One poster asked whether tweezing or plucking was the better route for avoiding ingrown hairs and a visibly altered look, and was pointed to a longer guide and to videos showing brows of similar density.[13][7] Another thread asked whether brow waxing gave a general lift to the face; the original poster said it had for them, and a reply advised plucking only the upper side.[2]

Poster concerns recur across threads: removing too much, hairs that regrow slowly after plucking, ingrown hairs and brows that look obviously worked on.[13] One poster describes their usual routine as removing a small amount of unibrow hair at the bridge and asks about also clearing hairs beneath the end of the arch.[13]

Wikipedia lists brushes, pencils, gels and powders as ways to define, fill or add fullness to brows, which users can apply daily without commitment.[4] The effect is immediate and washes off, which is why it is often a first step before semi-permanent options.
Threads discuss using castor oil on the brows, including which type to buy.[8] Results are reported anecdotally and no clinical trials of castor oil for eyebrow growth have been published.

A prescription route exists for eyelashes: the prostaglandin analogue bimatoprost (sold as Latisse) is cosmetically approved for underdeveloped lashes, and Wikipedia reports that the only eyebrow evidence it cites is a single case report of a 60-year-old woman who applied a 0.03 percent solution daily for eight months and noted thicker brow hairs.[14] Its listed adverse effects include eye redness and darkening of the eyelid skin.[14]

Microblading is a semi-permanent technique in which a technician uses a handheld tool with tiny needles to deposit pigment in hair-like strokes. Because the pigment sits in the upper dermis it fades faster than machine-applied tattooing. A session can last up to two years depending on pigment, sun exposure and skin type, with a touch-up suggested after about six weeks and then every 12 to 18 months.[5]

Wikipedia traces eyebrow tattooing to medical use for disguising brow hair loss, growth in cosmetic use in the US and parts of Asia in the 1980s and 1990s, and a hand-stroke "eyebrow embroidery" boom that started in Singapore around 2007 and reached North America by the mid-2010s.[5] Reported problems include migrating or changing-colour pigment, reactions to pigment ingredients and granulomas, and it is not regulated federally in the United States.[5]

Eyebrow transplantation moves follicles, usually from the back of the head, into bare areas, similar to scalp hair transplantation. Wikipedia lists people with genetically thin brows or who have over-tweezed as candidates, and compares healing to that of a tattoo with possible bruising and crusting.[4] Surgeons in Japan used small follicular-unit grafts to repair damaged eyebrows and lashes in the 1930s, and follicular unit extraction was described in 2002.[6]

Published reports include a 2020 case series of 352 patients with eyebrow loss treated with single-follicular-unit transplants and followed for four years, in which 91 percent had well-grown hair with a satisfactory direction and appearance, 5 percent were sparse at first but later satisfied, and no one had obvious donor-site scarring.[15] Other journals have published reports on follicular unit extraction for scarred or burned brows.

sections.h: Research on brow position and perception
paras: A 2007 study in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery morphed three eyebrow variations onto seven female portraits and had 357 people aged 12 to 85 rank them. Younger participants (up to 30) preferred lower brows and rejected arched ones, whereas those over 50 showed the opposite preference, leading the authors to conclude that no single ideal exists and that it depends on the age of the beholder.[10]

A 2023 Dermatologic Surgery survey of 652 responders ranked five brow shapes (Anastasia, head-up, horizontal, rounded, tail-up) on edited photos grouped by age, gender and self-reported ethnicity. Responders generally preferred the arched Anastasia shape, though not in every subgroup, with preferences stronger for female faces than male ones; the authors recommended asking each patient about their own preference.[16]

A 2025 rating study of 2,081 participants viewed a unisex face with nine combinations of brow and lateral-canthal height. Higher brows lowered rated attractiveness, femininity and trustworthiness and raised rated masculinity, dominance, threat and disgust, especially among female raters, and raising the outer eye corner had similar effects.[11] This is the research closest to the community's low-set-brow view, although it concerns raised brows in a unisex model and not grooming.

In Japan, hikimayu, removing the natural brows and painting new ones higher on the forehead, began in the 8th century as the court adopted Chinese customs and was most common in the Heian period, with a ban in 1870.[12] Wikipedia notes that some high-status women in the Elizabethan era removed their brows and that thin, plucked brows returned in the 1920s and 1930s, with Joan Crawford named as a 1930s example, while Audrey Hepburn is noted for thick brows.[4] Surgical brow lifts have an early published description dated to 1919, and toxin-based brow lifts were used from the 1970s.[4]

Eyebrow work is often presented as a low-cost step. Users post combined transformations, for example a thread pairing neck training with brow changes,[9] and ask whether brow work and skin colouring could improve their overall rating.[17] Posters disagree about shape: some favour as low a brow as possible, others warn against thinning.[2][13] The wider community is the subject of criticism in media coverage as well as defence by some participants; Wikipedia records that some men report benefits such as dating success and peer approval alongside critique from commentators.[3]

Users worry that over-plucking can leave sparse patches that regrow slowly, and ingrown hairs are a recurring concern in threads.[13] Wikipedia notes that tweezing and waxing can be painful, though pain often lessens with time.[4] Microblading carries tattoo-type risks such as infection, pigment reactions and uneven fading, and transplant recovery includes bruising and crusting; transplants and tattooing are carried out by professionals.[4][5] Transplant complications described in the general literature include temporary shedding of transplanted hair and small scars at the donor site.[6]
No studies found on eyebrowmaxxing as a practice. Related research includes rating studies of brow shape and height[10][16][11] and case-series reports on eyebrow transplantation.[15]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, brows are discussed as a cheap, fast way to change how the eyes look, with guides and threads comparing shapes and methods.[1][13] The ideas below are the ones that recur most.[2][7]

claims.claim: A lower, cleaner brow makes the face look better
Trimming hairs under the tail keeps an alert, positive tilt
Castor oil helps brows grow thicker
Waxing the brows gives a face-wide improvement (a "halo")
Plucking can stop hairs growing back
Brow work can be a meaningful part of a transformation
Arched brows are the most attractive shape

timeline.event: Japanese hikimayu, removing natural brows and painting them higher on the forehead, begins.[12]
Earliest published description of a surgical eyebrow lift, according to Wikipedia.[4]
Thin, plucked brows return to fashion in the West.[4]
Japanese surgeons use small follicular-unit grafts to repair damaged eyebrows and lashes.[6]
Doctors begin using botulinum-type toxins to raise the brow temporarily.[4]
Cosmetic eyebrow tattooing becomes more common in the US and parts of Asia.[5]
Follicular unit extraction (FUE) is described for hair transplantation.[6]
Hand-stroke eyebrow embroidery becomes popular in Singapore; a study of 357 people finds brow preferences depend on age.[5][10]
Microblading spreads across the US and Canada.[5]
A Nature Ecology & Evolution study argues that eyebrows evolved mainly for communication.[4]
A 652-person survey finds responders generally prefer an arched brow shape.[16]
A 2,081-person study finds higher brows lower rated attractiveness and trustworthiness.[11]
